To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The number of errors in the Floating Gates is strongly affected by the programming voltage; (2) The number of Floating Gate error reduces with time, and the annealing rate depends on the temperature; (3) The annealing of the Floating Gate errors can be linked to the annealing of the threshold voltages of the single cells.

(1) Floating Gate errors in NAND and NOR Flash memories are annealed after exposure to TID; (2) the reduction in the total number of Floating Gate is linked to the evolution of threshold voltages of single cells; (3) the annealing of errors is strongly dependent on temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the understanding of the physics of the Floating Gate errors, and with their annealing.
the understanding of the physics of radiation effects in Flash memories, and how the understanding of the physical mechanisms can be exploited in order to design new mitigation strategies.
the understanding of the physics behind Floating Gate errors in order to develop a model for the annealing process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the number of Floating Gated errors is a function of the threshold voltage, the temperature, and the program level.
the Floating Gate errors in NAND Flash memories are stable and the number of Floating Gates errors does not depend on the program level or on temperature.
Floating Gate errors are not stable and they anneal at room temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Floating Gate annealing is a very slow and complex process.

the annealing of Floating Gates errors is due to the thermal recombination of the radiation induced traps in the oxide, and that the annealing is strongly dependent on the threshold voltage of the cell.
the Floating Gate errors are annealed by the same mechanism that is responsible for the annealing of the Single Event Upset (SEU) errors in SRAM cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of Floating Gates errors can be reduced in a large amount by post-radiation temperature annealing, but only if the program level is high enough.

the number of errors in a Flash memory exposed to Total Ionization Dose (TID) is strongly correlated with the evolution of the cell threshold voltage, which can be used to predict the post-radiated behavior of the device.
the number of Floating Gates errors is a function of the threshold voltage and the annealing process.
